name: iptables - Packet Counter for Scan Verification
description: Use iptables packet counters to measure exactly how many packets an nmap scan sends and receives. Set ACCEPT rules on INPUT and OUTPUT for the target, reset counters with -Z, run the scan, then read the counters. Lets you compare scan types (SYN vs connect vs UDP) in terms of packet noise before running against real targets.

steps.label: Run the nmap scan you want to measure
Reset counters again before next comparison scan

examples.label: Full comparison sequence against 192.168.50.149
examples.command: sudo iptables -I INPUT 1 -s 192.168.50.149 -j ACCEPT && sudo iptables -I OUTPUT 1 -d 192.168.50.149 -j ACCEPT && sudo iptables -Z

notes: iptables -Z resets the byte/packet counters for all chains without removing the rules. -vn -L shows the counters. Compare: nmap default (TCP SYN) vs nmap -sT (connect) vs nmap -sU to understand which scan type generates more traffic before using on production networks or noisy engagements. This is a local analysis technique — entirely on your Kali box, no impact on the target.

recommended.note: Run the nmap scan under test while iptables counters are live.
UDP scans generate significantly more packets — verify before running on restricted engagements.

defense.prerequisites: Local root/sudo access on the attacker's Kali machine. This technique makes no network calls — it is purely a local measurement tool.
defense.why_it_works: iptables maintains per-rule packet and byte counters. -I inserts a rule at position 1 (top of chain) so all matching traffic is counted before any other rule can drop it. -Z zeroes the counters atomically across all chains, giving a clean baseline. -vn -L prints the counters in numeric form (no DNS resolution). Because the ACCEPT rules are on the attacker's local machine, they do not touch the target at all.
defense.impact: No direct attack impact — this is a preparation and opsec-calibration technique. Knowing the packet cost of each scan type lets an operator choose the least-noisy option before engaging a real target.
defense.artifacts: None on the target. On the attacker: iptables rules remain until flushed (iptables -D INPUT 1, iptables -D OUTPUT 1) or the host reboots.
defense.prevention: N/A — this is a local attacker-side technique. Defenders cannot prevent an operator from measuring their own scan traffic.
